title: The Beautiful Lie of Coursework
author: David Didau
summary: Didau uses two recent high-profile interviews -- UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell's call for more practical, coursework-style GCSE assessment, and incoming Eton head Alistair Chirnside's defense of teacher-assessed and oral work -- as a foil for a broader argument that exams remain fairer than coursework despite their flaws. He first shows that several of Powell's examples misdescribe existing qualifications, arguing she conflates what is taught with how it is assessed. He then turns to Chirnside, rejecting the idea that AI-detection technology or closer teacher supervision can rescue coursework, since teachers' own interventions inevitably become part of a 'successful' submission and teachers are demonstrably prone to socioeconomic bias in marking. Didau argues that oral exams (vivas), if genuinely decisive evidence of understanding, actually undercut the case for written coursework rather than supporting it. The piece closes by previewing a paywalled continuation with seven specific reasons exams are fairer than coursework. Throughout, the argumentative throughline is that any assessment reform must be evaluated against how it performs in ordinary, under-resourced, bias-prone school systems -- not idealized ones.
points: AQA's GCSE PE already allocates 40% of marks to non-exam assessment and its Food Prep GCSE is 50% non-exam, undercutting Powell's claim that exams currently exclude practical competence.

Research cited shows teachers marked identical work more harshly when they believed the author came from a poorer background, which Didau treats as a structural argument against expanding teacher-judged coursework.
Didau argues AI-detection technology is unlikely to ever reliably outpace LLMs' ability to evade detection, undermining Chirnside's proposed technical fix.
The piece argues that if an oral viva can reliably demonstrate a student's understanding, that itself is evidence against needing written coursework at all, since the viva alone would suffice.

Didau notes that closer teacher monitoring of developing coursework does not prevent AI-generated ideas from entering student work, and it makes teachers' own interventions harder to separate from student achievement.
quotes: So far so good. Nobody really thinks the current state of GCSEs is good enough and reform of some sort is both inevitable and welcome. It's obviously correct that the ability to produce a written account of how to prepare a meal tells us nothing about whether a student can cook.

Unfortunately, some of Powell's examples misdescribe existing qualifications. For instance, AQA's GCSE PE already allocates 40 per cent to non-exam assessment, including practical performance in three activities.

His appeal to pandemic grades confuses the ability to award marks with evidence that those marks are dependable. Plainly, teachers can assess work, but the question is whether their judgements are sufficiently comparable across schools and sufficiently protected from bias and institutional pressure.

Chirnside suggests that technological developments will make AI use detectable: even while he acknowledges "we're not quite there yet". The likelihood that the ability to detect AI will reliably outstrip the capability of LLMs to remain undetectable seems naive.

So, if an oral exam can provide decisive evidence of competence, we should ask what the coursework itself actually adds. For my money, introducing vivas is an argument against introducing written coursework.

Now, there's no doubt that exams are flawed, but replacing them is only an improvement if the alternative is better. Coursework has to work in schools where support is unequal, teachers are susceptible to bias and results carry consequences for those awarding the marks.
